svg.text: Controlled drugs: why the rules are shaped the way they are
Every rule here exists because the drug is both genuinely needed and genuinely diverted.
The chain that must never break
Locked cupboard, one key holder per shift
Register with a running balance
Two nurses check, both sign
Count at every shift change
Any waste witnessed and recorded
The balance must equal the shelf. Always.
When the count is wrong
Do not adjust the register to fit the shelf.
Do not wait for the next shift to sort it.
Do not quietly replace the missing dose.
Report the discrepancy at once, in writing,
before you leave the ward.
Delay is what turns an error into suspicion.
The fear that harms patients: morphine and the dying
Opioids titrated against pain in a patient who is dying do not shorten life, and addiction is not a risk that
matters here. What does happen, routinely, is that families and staff withhold doses out of fear, and the
patient dies in pain that was entirely treatable. Under-treatment is the common error, not overdose.
Reading a patient on an opioid
Watch the respiratory rate and the level of sedation, in that order of usefulness — sedation deepens before
breathing slows, so an increasingly drowsy patient is the earlier warning. A rousable patient with a normal
rate whose pain is controlled is exactly where you want to be. Constipation is certain: prescribe for it
from the first dose rather than waiting for the problem to arrive.
